hints: Picture the halogens at room temperature, chlorine as a gas, bromine as a liquid and iodine as a solid. What does that tell you about how easily they evaporate?
Volatility falls down the group because bigger molecules have stronger London dispersion forces, so think about how boiling point changes from $\text{Cl}_2$ to $\text{I}_2$.
For oxidising power, remember an oxidiser gains electrons, so ask yourself which atom, small chlorine or large iodine, attracts an extra electron more strongly.
walkthrough:
**Think About Volatility First**

Think of volatility as how easily a substance turns into vapour. A gas is very volatile, a solid is much less volatile.

Trend you can see:
$$\text{Cl}_2\text{(g)} \rightarrow \text{Br}_2\text{(l)} \rightarrow \text{I}_2\text{(s)}$$

**Explain The Volatility Trend**

Going down Group 17, atoms get bigger with more electrons. That means stronger London dispersion forces between molecules.

Stronger forces mean higher boiling point and less easy evaporation. So volatility decreases from chlorine to iodine.

**Think About Oxidising Strength**

An oxidising agent oxidises others by taking electrons from them. It is itself reduced:
$$\text{X}_2 + 2\text{e}^- \rightarrow 2\text{X}^-$$
The better it is at gaining electrons, the stronger the oxidiser.

**Explain The Oxidising Trend**

Down the group, the atom gets larger and the outer shell gets further from the nucleus. Incoming electrons are less strongly attracted because of more shielding and greater distance.

So $\text{Cl}_2$ is the strongest oxidiser and $\text{I}_2$ is the weakest. Strength as oxidising agent decreases. Both properties decrease.

options.A: Correct. Volatility decreases because boiling point rises from $\text{Cl}_2$ to $\text{I}_2$ due to stronger London forces. Oxidising strength also decreases because larger atoms attract electrons less effectively.
options.B: Incorrect. Volatility decreasing is right, but oxidising strength increasing is wrong. Students sometimes mix this with the reducing strength of halide ions ($\text{Cl}^-$, $\text{Br}^-$, $\text{I}^-$), which does increase down the group.
options.C: Incorrect. Oxidising strength decreasing is right, but volatility increasing is wrong. This trap comes from confusing volatility with boiling point. Boiling point increases down the group, so volatility does the opposite and decreases.
options.D: Incorrect. Both trends are stated backwards. Neither volatility nor oxidising power increases from chlorine to iodine, both become smaller as atoms get larger.
